Well done anything ruins the flavor. Sorry I could help you maybe try it meduim or rare

There's two sides to a good well done. The first way is the easy way, buy the fattiest type of burger meat you can find. 80% lean is usually pretty safe, but if you buy some cheap frozen box burgers they sometimes drop down lower. With that much fat it's almost impossible to ruin, even well done.

 

Now, real technique wise. The trick is to cook it slow, and to use a meat thermometer to determine when it's finished cooking in order to pull the burger off before it reaches well done. (Meat continues to cook once off the grill.) Cooking slowly will ensure an evenly cooked burger that will not dry out. It's not easy to do, and personally my voat is goes to the fatty burger that's idiot proof.

Yes, I do.

When you go to make your patty, mix a small amount of honey in it and whatever seasoning you want to add if any, mix it up well. Make the patty somewhat thin, maybe the thickness of your thumb. Make it as even and symmetrical as you can manage (perfection isn't the goal, don't worry).

Put a tablespoon of butter in the pan and melt it before you put the patty in (I'm assuming you are using lean beef because you don't want to drink your burger). Turn the heat up on high and let it heat up. You don't want it to stay at high heat very long, so pay attention. Once the pan is nice and hot, put the patty in and count to 10, flip it and count to ten, remove it. Remove the pan from the heat and turn the heat down to about 40-45%.

Once the pan and burner are cooled/lower heat, place the patty and pan back on the burner.

Put a teaspoon of butter on top of the patty. What you want is to let the patty slowly cook. I usually let mine sit on one side for about 20 minutes then flip it, and put another teaspoon of butter and wait another 20. This makes the most tasty, flavorful, and tender burger patties I've ever seen cooked at home, and it honestly rivals most restaurants (this is very simple, so I don't feel like that is me bragging).
